claim: Periodontal disease is an age-associated disorder clinically defined by periodontal bone loss, inflammation of the specialized tissues that surround and support the tooth, and microbiome dysbiosis.
source: Periodontal disease is an age-associated disorder clinically defined by periodontal bone loss, inflammation of the specialized tissues that surround and support the tooth, and microbiome dysbiosis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about periodontal disease in the abstract.

claim: Currently, there is no therapy for reversing periodontal disease, and treatment is generally restricted to preventive measures or tooth extraction.
source: Currently, there is no therapy for reversing periodontal disease, and treatment is generally restricted to preventive measures or tooth extraction.
evidence: This is stated as current clinical knowledge about periodontal disease treatment options.

claim: The FDA-approved drug rapamycin slows aging and extends lifespan in multiple organisms, including mice.
source: The FDA-approved drug rapamycin slows aging and extends lifespan in multiple organisms, including mice.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about rapamycin's effects, supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Short-term treatment with rapamycin rejuvenates the aged oral cavity of elderly mice, including regeneration of periodontal bone.
source: Here, we demonstrate that short-term treatment with rapamycin rejuvenates the aged oral cavity of elderly mice, including regeneration of periodontal bone, attenuation of gingival and periodontal bone inflammation, and revertive shift of the oral microbiome toward a more youthful composition.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Short-term treatment with rapamycin attenuates gingival and periodontal bone inflammation in elderly mice.
source: Here, we demonstrate that short-term treatment with rapamycin rejuvenates the aged oral cavity of elderly mice, including regeneration of periodontal bone, attenuation of gingival and periodontal bone inflammation, and revertive shift of the oral microbiome toward a more youthful composition.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data on inflammatory markers.

claim: Short-term treatment with rapamycin causes a revertive shift of the oral microbiome toward a more youthful composition in elderly mice.
source: Here, we demonstrate that short-term treatment with rapamycin rejuvenates the aged oral cavity of elderly mice, including regeneration of periodontal bone, attenuation of gingival and periodontal bone inflammation, and revertive shift of the oral microbiome toward a more youthful composition.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data.

claim: Old age is associated with failure to maintain homeostasis resulting in degradation of cellular maintenance and repair processes.
source: Old age is associated with failure to maintain homeostasis resulting in degradation of cellular maintenance and repair processes (López-Otín et al., 2013) and is the single greatest risk factor for many human diseases including cardiovascular disorders, dementias, diabetes, and most cancers (Kennedy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to López-Otín et al., 2013.

claim: Old age is the single greatest risk factor for many human diseases including cardiovascular disorders, dementias, diabetes, and most cancers.
source: Old age is associated with failure to maintain homeostasis resulting in degradation of cellular maintenance and repair processes (López-Otín et al., 2013) and is the single greatest risk factor for many human diseases including cardiovascular disorders, dementias, diabetes, and most cancers (Kennedy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kennedy et al., 2014.

claim: Interventions that target specific aging hallmarks have been shown to delay or prevent age-related disorders and extend lifespan in model organisms.
source: Interventions that target specific aging hallmarks have been shown to delay or prevent age-related disorders and extend lifespan in model organisms (Kaeberlein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kaeberlein et al., 2015.

claim: Rapamycin directly inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex I (mTORC1).
source: Rapamycin, an FDA-approved drug, which directly inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex I (mTORC1), is one such intervention that extends lifespan and ameliorates a variety of age-related phenotypes (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about rapamycin's mechanism of action, supported by citation.

claim: Rapamycin extends lifespan and ameliorates a variety of age-related phenotypes.
source: Rapamycin, an FDA-approved drug, which directly inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex I (mTORC1), is one such intervention that extends lifespan and ameliorates a variety of age-related phenotypes (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2013.

claim: In mice, rapamycin extends lifespan when administered beginning at 9 or 20 months of age.
source: In mice, rapamycin extends lifespan when administered beginning at 9 or 20 months of age (Harrison et al., 2009), and short-term treatments ranging from 6 to 12 weeks during adulthood have been shown to increase lifespan (Bitto et al., 2016), improve cardiac function (Flynn et al., 2013; Dai et al., 2014) and restore immune function as measured by vaccine response (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harrison et al., 2009.

claim: Short-term rapamycin treatments ranging from 6 to 12 weeks during adulthood have been shown to increase lifespan in mice.
source: In mice, rapamycin extends lifespan when administered beginning at 9 or 20 months of age (Harrison et al., 2009), and short-term treatments ranging from 6 to 12 weeks during adulthood have been shown to increase lifespan (Bitto et al., 2016), improve cardiac function (Flynn et al., 2013; Dai et al., 2014) and restore immune function as measured by vaccine response (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bitto et al., 2016.

claim: Short-term rapamycin treatments improve cardiac function in mice.
source: In mice, rapamycin extends lifespan when administered beginning at 9 or 20 months of age (Harrison et al., 2009), and short-term treatments ranging from 6 to 12 weeks during adulthood have been shown to increase lifespan (Bitto et al., 2016), improve cardiac function (Flynn et al., 2013; Dai et al., 2014) and restore immune function as measured by vaccine response (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Flynn et al., 2013 and Dai et al., 2014.

claim: Short-term rapamycin treatments restore immune function as measured by vaccine response in mice.
source: In mice, rapamycin extends lifespan when administered beginning at 9 or 20 months of age (Harrison et al., 2009), and short-term treatments ranging from 6 to 12 weeks during adulthood have been shown to increase lifespan (Bitto et al., 2016), improve cardiac function (Flynn et al., 2013; Dai et al., 2014) and restore immune function as measured by vaccine response (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2009.

claim: Initial indications suggest that mTORC1 inhibition may reverse declines in age-related heart function in companion dogs.
source: Initial indications suggest that mTORC1 inhibition may also reverse declines in age-related heart function in companion dogs (Urfer et al., 2017a; Urfer et al., 2017b), and age-related immune function (Mannick et al., 2014; Mannick et al., 2018) and skin aging (Chung et al., 2019) in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Urfer et al., 2017a and 2017b.

claim: Initial indications suggest that mTORC1 inhibition may reverse age-related immune function decline in humans.
source: Initial indications suggest that mTORC1 inhibition may also reverse declines in age-related heart function in companion dogs (Urfer et al., 2017a; Urfer et al., 2017b), and age-related immune function (Mannick et al., 2014; Mannick et al., 2018) and skin aging (Chung et al., 2019) in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mannick et al., 2014 and 2018.

claim: Initial indications suggest that mTORC1 inhibition may reverse skin aging in humans.
source: Initial indications suggest that mTORC1 inhibition may also reverse declines in age-related heart function in companion dogs (Urfer et al., 2017a; Urfer et al., 2017b), and age-related immune function (Mannick et al., 2014; Mannick et al., 2018) and skin aging (Chung et al., 2019) in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2019.

claim: Periodontal disease is clinically defined by inflammation of the periodontium, the specialized tissue surrounding and supporting the tooth structure, resulting in clinical attachment loss, alveolar (periodontal) bone loss and periodontal pocketing, and pathogenic changes in the oral microbiome.
source: Periodontal disease is clinically defined by inflammation of the periodontium, the specialized tissue surrounding and supporting the tooth structure, resulting in clinical attachment loss, alveolar (periodontal) bone loss and periodontal pocketing, and pathogenic changes in the oral microbiome (Könönen et al., 2019; Lang and Bartold, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Könönen et al., 2019 and Lang and Bartold, 2018.

claim: More than 60% of adults aged 65 years and older in the U.S. population have periodontitis.
source: Most recent epidemiologic data in the U.S. population suggests that more than 60% of adults aged 65 years and older have periodontitis (Eke et al., 2012; Eke et al., 2015), and diagnosis with periodontal disease is associated with increased risk for other age-related conditions including heart disease, diabetes, and Alzheimer's disease (Gil-Montoya et al., 2015; Kim and Amar, 2006; Razak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eke et al., 2012 and 2015.

claim: Diagnosis with periodontal disease is associated with increased risk for other age-related conditions including heart disease, diabetes, and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Most recent epidemiologic data in the U.S. population suggests that more than 60% of adults aged 65 years and older have periodontitis (Eke et al., 2012; Eke et al., 2015), and diagnosis with periodontal disease is associated with increased risk for other age-related conditions including heart disease, diabetes, and Alzheimer's disease (Gil-Montoya et al., 2015; Kim and Amar, 2006; Razak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gil-Montoya et al., 2015; Kim and Amar, 2006; and Razak et al., 2014.

claim: Periodontal disease shows a similar age-related risk profile as other age-associated diseases.
source: Given that periodontal disease shows a similar age-related risk profile as other age-associated diseases (An et al., 2018), we predicted that interventions which target biological aging could be effective at treating periodontal disease.
evidence: This is supported by citation to An et al., 2018.

claim: Aged mice treated with rapamycin have greater levels of periodontal bone than control animals.
source: Consistent with that hypothesis, aged mice treated with rapamycin have greater levels of periodontal bone than control animals (An et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to An et al., 2017.

claim: 8 weeks of treatment with rapamycin in aged mice is sufficient to regrow periodontal bone.
source: Here we report that 8 weeks of treatment with rapamycin in aged mice is sufficient to regrow periodontal bone, reduce inflammation in both gingival tissue and periodontal bone, and revert the composition of the oral microbiome back toward a more youthful state.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by microCT data.

claim: 8 weeks of treatment with rapamycin in aged mice is sufficient to reduce inflammation in both gingival tissue and periodontal bone.
source: Here we report that 8 weeks of treatment with rapamycin in aged mice is sufficient to regrow periodontal bone, reduce inflammation in both gingival tissue and periodontal bone, and revert the composition of the oral microbiome back toward a more youthful state.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by western blot and cytokine array data.

claim: 8 weeks of treatment with rapamycin in aged mice is sufficient to revert the composition of the oral microbiome back toward a more youthful state.
source: Here we report that 8 weeks of treatment with rapamycin in aged mice is sufficient to regrow periodontal bone, reduce inflammation in both gingival tissue and periodontal bone, and revert the composition of the oral microbiome back toward a more youthful state.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data.

claim: There was a significant loss of periodontal bone with age in the NIA-UW cohort.
source: As expected, there was a significant loss of periodontal bone with age in the NIA-UW cohort (Figure 2, A to C).
evidence: This is supported by microCT measurements shown in Figure 2, A to C.

claim: Mice treated with rapamycin for 8 weeks had significantly more bone at the end of the treatment period compared to mice that received the control diet (eudragit).
source: Mice treated with rapamycin for 8 weeks had significantly more bone at the end of the treatment period compared to mice that received the control diet (eudragit) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by microCT measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Old mice randomized into either the eudragit control or rapamycin treatment groups had significantly less periodontal bone than young mice prior to the treatment period in the JAX cohort.
source: Old mice randomized into either the eudragit control or rapamycin treatment groups had significantly less periodontal bone than young mice prior to the treatment period (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by microCT measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: After 8 weeks, the rapamycin treated mice had significantly more periodontal bone compared to eudragit controls in the JAX cohort.
source: After 8 weeks, the rapamycin treated mice had significantly more periodontal bone compared to eudragit controls and also compared to the pre-treatment levels for the same animals (Figure 2, D to F).
evidence: This is supported by microCT measurements shown in Figure 2, D to F.

claim: After 8 weeks, the rapamycin treated mice had significantly more periodontal bone compared to the pre-treatment levels for the same animals in the JAX cohort.
source: After 8 weeks, the rapamycin treated mice had significantly more periodontal bone compared to eudragit controls and also compared to the pre-treatment levels for the same animals (Figure 2, D to F).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal microCT measurements shown in Figure 2, D to F.

claim: Normal bone homeostasis results from a balance between new bone growth and bone resorption, which is reflected by the ratio of RANKL to OPG.
source: Normal bone homeostasis results from a balance between new bone growth and bone resorption, which is reflected by the ratio of RANKL (receptor-activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand) to OPG (osteoprotegerin), and dysregulation of this balance contributes to bone loss in periodontitis (Darveau, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Darveau, 2010.

claim: Dysregulation of the RANKL to OPG balance contributes to bone loss in periodontitis.
source: Normal bone homeostasis results from a balance between new bone growth and bone resorption, which is reflected by the ratio of RANKL (receptor-activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand) to OPG (osteoprotegerin), and dysregulation of this balance contributes to bone loss in periodontitis (Darveau, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Darveau, 2010.

claim: Significantly greater levels of RANKL were detected in old animals of both cohorts compared to young animals.
source: Consistent with bone loss during aging, we detected significantly greater levels of RANKL in old animals of both cohorts compared to young animals (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: OPG levels remained relatively stable during aging, resulting in an increase in the RANKL:OPG ratio indicative of bone resorption exceeding bone formation.
source: OPG levels remained relatively stable, resulting in an increase in the RANKL:OPG ratio indicative of bone resorption exceeding bone formation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Age-associated defects in bone homeostasis were suppressed by eight weeks of rapamycin treatment.
source: These age-associated defects in bone homeostasis were suppressed by eight weeks of rapamycin treatment (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A significant increase in TRAP+ cells was observed in periodontal bone with age.
source: In addition to increased RANKL:OPG ratio, a significant increase in TRAP+ cells was also observed in periodontal bone with age (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase) is a histochemical marker of bone resorbing osteoclasts.
source: TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase) is a histochemical marker of bone resorbing osteoclasts (Hayman, 2008; Ballanti et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayman, 2008 and Ballanti et al., 1997.

claim: Rapamycin treatment for eight weeks decreased TRAP+ cells.
source: Rapamycin treatment for eight weeks also decreased TRAP+ cells.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Rapamycin reverses periodontal bone loss in the aging murine oral cavity at least in part through inhibition of bone resorption.
source: Together, our data indicate that rapamycin reverses periodontal bone loss in the aging murine oral cavity at least in part through inhibition of bone resorption.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on RANKL:OPG ratio and TRAP+ cells.

claim: Gingival inflammation is a defining feature of periodontal disease.
source: Along with bone loss, gingival inflammation is a defining feature of periodontal disease.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about periodontal disease.

claim: Aging is associated with chronic accumulation of pro-inflammatory factors, a collective term referred to as inflammaging.
source: Aging is also associated with chronic accumulation of pro-inflammatory factors, a collective term referred to as inflammaging (Chung et al., 2009; Franceschi and Ottaviani, 1997; Franceschi et al., 2000; De Martinis et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2009; Franceschi and Ottaviani, 1997; Franceschi et al., 2000; and De Martinis et al., 2005.

claim: The nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) is a hub of immune and inflammatory response activated both during normal aging and as a consequence of periodontal disease.
source: The nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) is a hub of immune and inflammatory response activated both during normal aging and as a consequence of periodontal disease (Arabaci et al., 2010; Ambili and Janam, 2017; Abu-Amer, 2013; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arabaci et al., 2010; Ambili and Janam, 2017; Abu-Amer, 2013; and Liu et al., 2017.

claim: IκBα functions as a negative regulator of NF-κB by sequestering it in the cytoplasm.
source: IκBα functions as a negative regulator of NF-κB by sequestering it in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NF-κB signaling.

claim: Degradation of IκBα or phosphorylated-IκBα leads to nuclear localization of NF-κB subunits which induce expression of target inflammatory genes, such as TNF-α and IL-1β.
source: Degradation of IκBα or phosphorylated-IκBα leads to nuclear localization of NF-κB subunits which induce expression of target inflammatory genes, such as TNF-α and IL-1β (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2017.

claim: In both the gingival tissue and periodontal bone, there was an increase in p65 expression with corresponding decrease of IκBα levels, indicating an age-associated increase in NF-κB inflammatory signaling in the periodontium.
source: In both the gingival tissue and periodontal bone, there was an increase in p65 expression with corresponding decrease of IκBα levels, indicating an age-associated increase in NF-κB inflammatory signaling in the periodontium (Figure 4, A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4, A and B.

claim: Eight weeks of rapamycin treatment was sufficient to reverse age-associated changes in NF-κB signaling.
source: Eight weeks of rapamycin treatment was sufficient to reverse these changes.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4, A and B.

claim: Elevated expression of several cytokines was found in both the gingival tissue and the periodontal bone during aging.
source: Consistent with the increase in NF-κB signaling, we found elevated expression of several cytokines in both the gingival tissue and the periodontal bone (Figure 4, E and F).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine array data shown in Figure 4, E and F.

claim: Eight weeks of rapamycin treatment reversed most age-associated chemokine and cytokine changes in both the gingival tissue and periodontal bone.
source: Eight weeks of rapamycin treatment reversed most age-associated chemokine and cytokine changes in both the gingival tissue and periodontal bone.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine array data shown in Figure 4, E and F.

claim: Transient treatment with rapamycin during middle-age can largely restore a youthful inflammatory state in both the gingiva and periodontal bone of mice.
source: Thus, transient treatment with rapamycin during middle-age can largely restore a youthful inflammatory state in both the gingiva and periodontal bone of mice (Wikham, 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the data on NF-κB signaling and cytokine expression.

claim: Dysbiotic shifts in the oral microbiome are thought to play a significant role in the progression of periodontal disease in humans.
source: Dysbiotic shifts in the oral microbiome are thought to play a significant role in the progression of periodontal disease in humans.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about periodontal disease.

claim: Rapamycin treatment can remodel the gut microbiome in mice.
source: We and others have previously shown that rapamycin treatment can remodel the gut microbiome in mice (Bitto et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2016; Hurez et al., 2015); however, the effect of rapamycin on the oral microbiome has not been explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bitto et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2016; and Hurez et al., 2015.

claim: The effect of rapamycin on the oral microbiome has not been explored prior to this study.
source: We and others have previously shown that rapamycin treatment can remodel the gut microbiome in mice (Bitto et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2016; Hurez et al., 2015); however, the effect of rapamycin on the oral microbiome has not been explored.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: Examination of the alpha diversity of the oral cavity illustrated a significant increase in species richness during aging that rapamycin attenuated.
source: Examination of the alpha diversity of the oral cavity illustrated a significant increase in species richness during aging that rapamycin attenuated (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Among the most notable alterations in taxonomic abundance between groups was the reduction of Bacteroidetes phylum in the rapamycin-treated old animals.
source: Among the most notable alterations in taxonomic abundance between groups was the reduction of Bacteroidetes phylum in the rapamycin-treated old animals (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When pooled across sites, no significant difference was observed between levels of Bacteroidetes in untreated young animals and old animals treated with rapamycin.
source: When pooled across sites, no significant difference was observed between levels of Bacteroidetes in untreated young animals and old animals treated with rapamycin.
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: Old animals treated with rapamycin in the JAX cohort had even lower levels of Bacteroidetes than young untreated mice (p<0.05).
source: Old animals treated with rapamycin in the JAX cohort had even lower levels of Bacteroidetes than young untreated mice (p<0.05), whereas in the UW cohort rapamycin treatment lowered the levels of Bacteroidetes to the level of the young mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the UW cohort rapamycin treatment lowered the levels of Bacteroidetes to the level of the young mice.
source: Old animals treated with rapamycin in the JAX cohort had even lower levels of Bacteroidetes than young untreated mice (p<0.05), whereas in the UW cohort rapamycin treatment lowered the levels of Bacteroidetes to the level of the young mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Bacteroidetes phylum consists of over 7000 different species.
source: The Bacteroidetes phylum consists of over 7000 different species (Thomas et al., 2011) and includes bacteria associated with human periodontal disease such as Porphyromonas gingivalis, Treponema denticola, and Bacteroides forsythus (van Winkelhoff et al., 2002; Torres et al., 2019; Socransky et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2011.

claim: The Bacteroidetes phylum includes bacteria associated with human periodontal disease such as Porphyromonas gingivalis, Treponema denticola, and Bacteroides forsythus.
source: The Bacteroidetes phylum consists of over 7000 different species (Thomas et al., 2011) and includes bacteria associated with human periodontal disease such as Porphyromonas gingivalis, Treponema denticola, and Bacteroides forsythus (van Winkelhoff et al., 2002; Torres et al., 2019; Socransky et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van Winkelhoff et al., 2002; Torres et al., 2019; and Socransky et al., 1998.

claim: Both the Firmicutes and Proteobacteria phyla showed a significant difference that was age dependent but was not significantly altered by rapamycin treatment.
source: Further, both the Firmicutes and Proteobacteria phyla also showed a significant difference that was age dependent (Figure 5B) but was not significantly altered by rapamycin treatment.
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A significant separation of the oral microbiome was discovered between old control and old rapamycin-treated animals using weighted UniFrac distances.
source: We discovered a significant separation of the oral microbiome between old control and old rapamycin-treated animals, while no significant differences were observed between young mice and old rapamycin-treated mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by beta diversity analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the oral microbiome between young mice and old rapamycin-treated mice using weighted UniFrac distances.
source: We discovered a significant separation of the oral microbiome between old control and old rapamycin-treated animals, while no significant differences were observed between young mice and old rapamycin-treated mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by beta diversity analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No significant differences were observed in alpha diversity, beta diversity, nor relative taxonomic abundance between young untreated mice and old mice treated with rapamycin.
source: Overall, we observed no significant differences in alpha diversity, beta diversity, nor relative taxonomic abundance between young untreated mice and old mice treated with rapamycin, suggesting an eight-week treatment with rapamycin reverted the old oral microbiome to a more youthful state.
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: An eight-week treatment with rapamycin reverted the old oral microbiome to a more youthful state.
source: Overall, we observed no significant differences in alpha diversity, beta diversity, nor relative taxonomic abundance between young untreated mice and old mice treated with rapamycin, suggesting an eight-week treatment with rapamycin reverted the old oral microbiome to a more youthful state.
evidence: This is inferred from the microbiome data showing similarity between young and rapamycin-treated old mice.

claim: No batch effect was detected when comparing the JAX and NIA-UW cohorts (PERMANOVA, nperm = 999, p=0.34).
source: Despite differences in animal facility and diet composition, no batch effect was detected when comparing the JAX and NIA-UW cohorts (PERMANOVA, nperm = 999, p=0.34) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: A short-term treatment with rapamycin in aged mice is sufficient to reverse three clinically defining features of periodontal disease: periodontal bone loss, periodontal inflammation, and pathogenic changes to the oral microbiome.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that a short-term treatment with rapamycin in aged mice is sufficient to reverse three clinically defining features of periodontal disease: periodontal bone loss, periodontal inflammation, and pathogenic changes to the oral microbiome.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings supported by all the experimental data.

claim: This work adds further support for the Geroscience Hypothesis, which posits that any intervention which targets the biological aging process will simultaneously delay multiple age-related diseases and functional declines.
source: This adds further support for the Geroscience Hypothesis, which posits that any intervention which targets the biological aging process will simultaneously delay multiple age-related diseases and functional declines (Kaeberlein, 2017; Sierra and Kohanski, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kaeberlein, 2017 and Sierra and Kohanski, 2017, and inferred from the study findings.

claim: This is the first report of rejuvenation in the aged oral cavity.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of rejuvenation in the aged oral cavity.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Improvements in age-related cardiac function associated with a similar rapamycin treatment regimen have been found to persist for at least eight weeks following cessation of treatment.
source: Improvements in age-related cardiac function associated with a similar rapamycin treatment regimen have been found to persist for at least eight weeks following cessation of treatment (Quarles et al., 2020), and it will be of interest to determine whether similar outcomes are observed for improvements in oral health.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Quarles et al., 2020.

claim: It will be important to determine whether the effects of rapamycin on the aged periodontium will persist after the treatment period or will rapidly revert back to the aged state.
source: One such question is whether the effects of rapamycin on the aged periodontium will persist after the treatment period or will rapidly revert back to the aged state.
evidence: This is stated as a future research question.

claim: It will be important to determine whether the effects of rapamycin are mediated through local inhibition of mTORC1 in the gingiva and periodontal bone or through systemic effects on immune function or other tissues.
source: It will also be important in future studies to determine whether these effects are mediated through local inhibition of mTORC1 in the gingiva and periodontal bone or through systemic effects on immune function or other tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a future research question.

claim: It will be of interest to understand whether additional features of oral health that are known to decline with age, such as salivary function, are improved by rapamycin treatment.
source: Likewise, it will be of interest to understand whether additional features of oral health that are known to decline with age, such as salivary function, are improved by rapamycin treatment.
evidence: This is stated as a future research question.

claim: Additional geroscience interventions, such clearance of senescent cells, may phenocopy the effects of rapamycin in the oral cavity.
source: Finally, these results suggest the intriguing likelihood that additional geroscience interventions, such clearance of senescent cells, may phenocopy the effects of rapamycin in this context.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis based on the study findings.

claim: Such interventions could pave the way for the first effective treatments to reverse periodontal disease and improve oral health in the elderly.
source: Such interventions could pave the way for the first effective treatments to reverse periodontal disease and improve oral health in the elderly.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative future application of the findings.

claim: Experiments were performed on two different cohorts housed at two sites: the University of Washington in Seattle, WA and the Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor, ME.
source: To enhance rigor and reproducibility, experiments were performed on two different cohorts housed at two sites: the University of Washington in Seattle, WA and the Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor, ME.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological approach to enhance rigor.

claim: Mice were treated at both sites with encapsulated rapamycin (eRAPA) in the diet at 42ppm, which has been shown to significantly increase lifespan of UMHET3 and C57BL6/J mice.
source: We then treated mice at both sites with encapsulated rapamycin (eRAPA) in the diet at 42ppm, which has been shown to significantly increase lifespan of UMHET3 and C57BL6/J mice (Miller et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014), or control food (eudragit).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2014 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: All data are from female mice, which have previously been found to have greater increases in lifespan and some health metrics compared to male mice at this dose of rapamycin.
source: All data are from female mice, which have previously been found to have greater increases in lifespan and some health metrics compared to male mice at this dose of rapamycin (Miller et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2014 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: For this study, young, adult, and old mice were 6, 13, and 20 months of age, respectively.
source: For this study, young, adult, and old mice were 6, 13, and 20 months of age, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail.

claim: Periodontal bone loss was measured as distance from the cementoenamel junction (CEJ) to the alveolar bone crest (ABC) on 16 predetermined landmarks on the buccal aspect of maxillary and mandibular periodontium.
source: Periodontal bone loss was measured as distance from the cementoenamel junction (CEJ) to the alveolar bone crest (ABC) on 16 predetermined landmarks on the buccal aspect of maxillary and mandibular periodontium.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The presence of new bone following rapamycin treatment can be observed by comparison of μCT images from the same animals before and after treatment.
source: The presence of new bone following rapamycin treatment can be observed by comparison of μCT images from the same animals before and after treatment (Figure 2, D and E).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal microCT imaging shown in Figure 2, D and E.

claim: The increase in periodontal bone upon rapamycin treatment reflects growth of new bone rather than just attenuation of bone loss.
source: To determine whether the increase in periodontal bone upon rapamycin treatment reflects attenuation of bone loss or growth of new bone, we performed μCT imaging on mice before and after treatment in the JAX cohort (Figure 1A). Old mice randomized into either the eudragit control or rapamycin treatment groups had significantly less periodontal bone than young mice prior to the treatment period (Figure 2F). After 8 weeks, the rapamycin treated mice had significantly more periodontal bone compared to eudragit controls and also compared to the pre-treatment levels for the same animals (Figure 2, D to F).
evidence: This is inferred from the longitudinal data showing bone increase compared to pre-treatment levels in the same animals.
